description: At FireData we are made up of a multidisciplinary team from diverse universities (UACH, TECNM Delicias, UTCH BIS) and cities in México (Chihuahua, Delicias, Jiménez) , sharing a passion for innovation and creativity that combines software with IoT.
summary: FireData is a web app that uses NASA FIRMS satellite fire data to build a consistent burning calendar for any region, from 2002 to today. Our goal is to help fire managers, brigades and researchers in underserved regions see when and where fires really happen. By calibrating NASA's newer VIIRS sensor to match the older MODIS record, region by region, FireData lets users pick an area, see which months and years burned the most, compare this month with the historical median, and download the data. The platform also connects our "estaca", a low-cost ESP32 field station that reports temperature, humidity, pressure, flame and sound from the ground, between satellite passes. FireData addresses the false jump in fire counts that appears when the two sensors are mixed, and we demonstrate it across all 32 states of Mexico. It would help communities worldwide tell a real fire anomaly from a sensor change, and act earlier.
details: FireData was built in two parts. The harmonization pipeline, written in Python with NumPy and pandas, processes 5.4 million NASA FIRMS hotspots from MODIS and VIIRS across Mexico's 32 states, clipped to INEGI's official boundaries. It unifies the formats, maps MODIS brightness onto the VIIRS scale, and groups VIIRS pixels into MODIS-sized cells, using a fire-power threshold fitted for each state so that both sensors count fires the same way (4.8% error on years never used for fitting). One flag column marks the consistent series, and no original row is deleted. The results are stored in SQLite and served by a FastAPI backend on AWS EC2, which also pulls near-real-time detections and vegetation layers from NASA GIBS and weather from NASA POWER and Open-Meteo. The web app, built with Next.js, React, TypeScript and Leaflet and hosted on GitHub Pages, shows the burning calendar by state or drawn area, the historical median, an interactive map and CSV downloads, with a lightweight mode for slow rural connections. LightGBM models piloted in Chihuahua forecast fire risk for the next 3 days (from recent detections, NASA POWER weather and vegetation) and for the next 7 to 28 days (from the harmonized record), and they beat seasonal baselines on years they never saw, most clearly up to 14 days ahead. Our ESP32 "estaca" prototype, programmed with Arduino-style firmware, sends temperature, humidity, pressure, flame and sound readings to the same backend. Together, these pieces turn two incompatible satellite records into one fire history that any region can rebuild with free NASA data.
